questions.text: Context // Read Isaiah 8:20-22. How is it related to the descriptions found in 9:1-2? (Note: the places described in v1a and 1b all refer to the same regions, which were the first places in the northern kingdom of Israel to fall to Assyrian empire around 733 BC.)

Observation // From vv1-3, contrast the previous and future conditions of the places described. From vv4-6, what are the three reasons given for this change in circumstances? Which of these is the main reason? (Hint: read "for" to mean "because")

Meaning // This week's Advent theme is Hope. How does today's passage point us to Hope? How would the arrival of the prophesied child and his reign secure this hope? (Think about the descriptions in vv6b-7.)

Application // Jesus is the ultimate fulfilment of Isaiah's prophecy. Read John 1:1-5, 9-13. Have you come to believe in Jesus as the true Hope and Light of the world who gives life and enables you to become a child of God? Take time to give thanks to God for giving us the hope that is found in Jesus alone.

devotionals.title: Hope In A God Who Acts (by Pr Evangeline Chong)
devotionals.passageText:
1 Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down,
    that the mountains might quake at your presence—
2 as when fire kindles brushwood
    and the fire causes water to boil—
to make your name known to your adversaries,
    and that the nations might tremble at your presence!
3 When you did awesome things that we did not look for,
    you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence.
4 From of old no one has heard
    or perceived by the ear,
no eye has seen a God besides you,
    who acts for those who wait for him.
5 You meet him who joyfully works righteousness,
    those who remember you in your ways.
Behold, you were angry, and we sinned;
    in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?
6 We have all become like one who is unclean,
    and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.
We all fade like a leaf,
    and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.
7 There is no one who calls upon your name,
    who rouses himself to take hold of you;
for you have hidden your face from us,
    and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities.

8 But now, O Lord, you are our Father;
    we are the clay, and you are our potter;
    we are all the work of your hand.
9 Be not so terribly angry, O Lord,
    and remember not iniquity forever.
    Behold, please look, we are all your people.
devotionals.article: When you did awesome things that we did not look for, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. Isaiah 64:3-4 In Israel's history, God's coming down to Mount Sinai (Exodus 19) marked the presence of God in their midst. With thunder, lightning and a dense cloud, the holy God descended to speak to His people and prepare them for a new life in His presence after their freedom from slavery in Egypt. In this prayer (following the prophecies of the punishment of exile to Assyria in Chap 1-39 and Babylon in Chap 40-55), Isaiah cries out in distress to God who judges sin yet draws near to act for the good of Israel. Earlier, Isaiah had prophesied God's promised action: "the Lord himself will give you a sign: The virgin will conceive and give birth to a son, and will call him Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14). And we now know that God was preparing to act for those in distress! Doing the most unthinkable thing, He sent Jesus to the cross to give humanity a way out of our sins and reconcile us to Himself. As we begin the season of Advent, a time of reflection on Jesus' promised arrival, both in memory of His incarnation and in anticipation of His return in glory, let us keep our eyes open to see what God is doing, acting in power and love for the good of our world and in our lives. Let us hold on to the hope of a God "who acts for those who wait for Him" (v4) and who will come down again to dwell among His people again.

devotionals.title: Hope In A God Who Is Faithful (by Pr Evangeline Chong)
devotionals.passageText:
3 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

4 I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, 5 that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge— 6 even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— 7 so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ, 8 who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
devotionals.article:
In 2000, a Barna survey showed that 75% agreed that the Bible teaches that "God only helps those who help themselves." This idea has roots in ancient Greek thought and Algernon Sidney gave it its form in 1698, yet it could not be further from the truth. The Asian culture of distant fathers and virtues of self-reliance and perseverance feed even more into this notion. No wonder many children of God who acknowledge Jesus only as Savior, struggle and fight as much as the rest of the world to fend and provide for themselves, living like spiritual orphans as if the God who calls Himself their Father is not interested in their daily lives. As such, many see a relationship with God as just merely a church routine of ever-growing expectations of prayer, faith and activity without knowing the faithful God. 
Yet 1 Corinthians begins with reminding God's people of the glorious hope they have in Christ where the church has been given all things it needs: Grace of God (v4), riches in God (all speech and knowledge v5), all gifts (v7). On top of all these, as we await Jesus' second Advent, we have a great Savior who will sustain us guiltless to the end (v8). 
Our God, the "Father to the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5) is faithful, not a neglectful parent who only drops in to check our homework. He is a God who helped the "utterly helpless, (for) Christ came at just the right time and died for us sinners (Romans 5:6 NLT)." He sent Jesus when no one was looking (Isaiah 64:3) so we can trust Him for the everyday and trust Jesus to return. This gives us a restedness in life and hope as we await the second advent of Jesus.
devotionals.prayer:
Father, thank you that in Christ I lack nothing and that you are faithful to the end.
Forgive me for living as though I must earn my place or provide for myself.
Teach me to rest in your grace and to wait with hope for the day Jesus returns. Amen.

devotionals.article:
Unlike most people I know, who prefer to sleep in complete darkness and would even go as far as using an eye mask to block out every bit of light, I've always felt more comfortable with a small light left on. Even a faint night light in the corner brings a quiet sense of peace and safety.

I wonder if you've ever felt that way, not just at night, but in life itself?  There are seasons when a shadow or darkness hangs over everything: worry about job security and the rising cost of living, pressure to keep up with work, studies, and family expectations, strained relationships, or burdens we carry in silence.  It can feel like being in a long, dark tunnel, with no light in sight, wondering when we'll finally come out the other side.

That is exactly where God's people stood when the prophet spoke these words in Isaiah 9:1—7. They lived in deep darkness — oppressed, afraid, and longing for hope. In the middle of the darkness, God gave a promise that brought hope:

"The people walking in darkness have seen a great light;
on those living in the land of deep darkness
a light has dawned." (Isaiah 9:2)

This wasn't a promise about a lamp beside a bed. It was the promise of Jesus — the Great Light who was coming to shine in our deepest shadows.  Isaiah tells us exactly who this Child is:

The Wonderful Counsellor who understands us completely.
The Mighty God who possesses the power to save and deliver us.
The Everlasting Father who loves and cares for us always.
The Prince of Peace who brings wholeness that the world cannot give. 

He came not only to show us the way, but to be the Way. He came to break the power of sin and fear, bring hope into our darkness, and establish a kingdom of peace that will never end.

Whatever darkness you may be facing today, remember this: the Light has already come. No darkness is too deep for Jesus. Whether you are struggling with fear, sadness, confusion, or sin, His light is greater than all of it. You do not need to fix your life before coming to Him. Come as you are and let His light shine into your situation.

But Jesus did not come only to shine His light on us. He calls us to walk in that light. Just as the people in Isaiah's day were invited to follow God's ways, we too are called to turn away from sin and follow Jesus each day through prayer, reading His Word, and obeying Him.

We will still face challenges, but we do not walk alone. Jesus goes before us, guides us, and strengthens us. As we keep our eyes on Him, His light will lead us through the darkness and fill our hearts with hope, peace, and joy.

devotionals.article: "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem." (Isaiah 40:1–2) Have you noticed how easily we lose our peace, even in church? A disagreement during a ministry meeting, an unkind remark, a misunderstanding between brothers and sisters, or simply the exhaustion of serving week after week. Sometimes we carry these frustrations home, replaying conversations in our minds. We wonder why serving God can be so tiring when we are supposed to be serving together in love. Into such restlessness, God speaks: "Comfort, comfort my people." What a surprising beginning! Israel had sinned, rebelled, and suffered the consequences of exile. Yet God did not begin with another rebuke. He spoke tenderly, announcing that her warfare had ended and her iniquity was pardoned. God's comfort does not come because His people have finally become good enough. It comes because He is gracious and faithful to His promises. Centuries later, Mark opens his Gospel by recalling Isaiah's words: "Prepare the way of the Lord." John the Baptist calls people to repentance, preparing them for the coming of Jesus Christ. The God who announces peace is the same God who comes to make that peace possible. Jesus, the Prince of Peace, does not wait for us to resolve every conflict, overcome every weakness, or put our lives in order before coming to us. He comes to bear our sins, reconcile us to God, and transform our hearts. Perhaps this Advent, as we prepare Christmas carolling outreach, worship services, and home visits, we need to hear God's tender voice before rushing into another season of activities. Some of us may be carrying disappointment with someone in church. Others may be struggling with guilt over something we have said or done. Still others may simply be tired. Listen again: "Comfort, comfort my people." The Shepherd who gathers His lambs in His arms (Isaiah 40:11) is the same Saviour who welcomes weary sinners. And perhaps, having received His tender comfort, we can begin speaking a little more tenderly to one another. After all, how can we announce the Prince of Peace to our neighbours if we refuse to receive and share His peace among ourselves? May this song bring you comfort, Peace be with you, 愿你平安! Click to watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YMPXK_wtJvI
devotionals.prayer: Our Father in heaven, thank You for speaking tenderly to us and welcoming us through Jesus Christ, even when we have sinned and fallen short. Quiet our restless hearts, heal our broken relationships, and teach us to extend the same grace and gentleness we have received from You. As we prepare to share the good news this Christmas, may Your peace first fill our hearts and then overflow into the lives of those around us. In Jesus� name, Amen.

8 But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. 9 The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. 10 But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.

11 Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, 12 waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! 13 But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.

14 Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. 15 And count the patience of our Lord as salvation
devotionals.article: �Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.� (Psalm 85:10, ESV) Why is God taking so long? Perhaps you have prayed for years for a loved one to come to Christ. You have invited them to church, shared the Gospel, and tried to live faithfully before them. Yet nothing seems to change. Or perhaps you have been praying for a broken relationship to be restored. You have taken the first step, apologised, forgiven, and waited. But the relationship remains strained. Even in our church, we long to see lives transformed, younger generations growing in faith, and more people joining us in God's mission. Yet sometimes progress seems so slow. We become restless, and we wonder whether God is doing anything at all. Peter reminds us that �with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day� (2 Peter 3:8). God's apparent delay is not indifference. It is patience. He does not wish that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. What we perceive as delay may be an expression of God's extraordinary mercy. Think of those whom we have been praying for in our families and neighbourhoods. Some have resisted the Gospel for decades. Yet God continues to give them opportunities to hear His Word and encounter His love. This Advent, as we go into homes to share the Christmas message, we may meet people who are indifferent, hesitant, or even resistant. We may wonder whether our visits make any difference. But God is patient, far more patient than we are. Psalm 85 gives us another beautiful picture of God's character: �Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.� God's peace is not achieved by ignoring sin or pretending that everything is fine. His love does not compromise His righteousness. His faithfulness does not abandon His justice. At the cross of Jesus Christ, we see these qualities come together. God does not overlook our sins; Christ bears their judgment. Through His sacrifice, sinners are reconciled to a holy God. We do not know when Christ will return. We cannot control how quickly someone responds to the Gospel, when a relationship will heal, or how our church will grow. But we know the character of the One who holds our future. Knowing Him changes the way we wait. We can continue praying for our loved ones without despair. We can keep reaching out to our neighbours without demanding immediate results. We can serve one another faithfully even when change is slow. This Advent, may we discover that peace grows not when God finally follows our timetable, but when our restless hearts learn to rest in His character. devotionals.prayer: Heavenly Father, forgive our impatience when Your answers seem slow and our prayers seem unanswered. Help us to rest in Your unfailing love, trusting that Your timing is always wise and Your patience is greater than ours. As we wait, grant us peace, teach us to persevere joyfully, and share the hope of Christ with those who have yet to know You. In Jesus� name, Amen.

devotionals.article:
Have you ever had a difficult day and found yourself becoming impatient with the people around you? Sometimes, when our hearts are troubled or we are holding on to hurt, it affects the way we speak and treat others. A small disagreement can easily turn into an argument when we react out of frustration. But when our hearts are resting in God's peace, we can respond with greater patience, kindness, and grace.

As we journey through Advent, we remember that Jesus came into a world filled with sin, hostility, and broken relationships. In Ephesians 2:11�18, Paul reminds us that through His death on the cross, Jesus broke down the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles and brought them together as one people.

Paul declares in verse 14, �For he himself is our peace.� What does this mean? It means that our peace is found not simply in having our problems resolved, but in Jesus Himself. Through His death on the cross brings peace in two directions:

First, Jesus brings us back to God. Our sin had separated us from Him, but through Jesus' death on the cross, He removed the barrier of sin that separated us from God so that we can be reconciled to God. We no longer need to hide from Him when we are struggling.

We can come to Him honestly, knowing that He welcomes us with His grace.

Second, Jesus brings us together with one another. Through Jesus� death on the cross, He broke down the walls of hostility that divided people. In Christ, people from different backgrounds are brought into one family. Our differences need not become walls that divide us. Instead, we are called to love one another and live in the unity that Christ has made possible.

Jesus does not merely give us peace; He Himself is the One through whom we are brought back to God and united as His people.

Because we have peace with God through Jesus, His peace can take root in our hearts and shape the way we face life�s difficulties. As we learn to rest in His love and trust in His faithfulness, His peac steadies our hearts and helps us respond to difficult situations with patience, grace, and kindness.

So, as we prepare to celebrate Jesus' birth this Advent, let us think about how we can live out His peace in our daily lives:

Examine our hearts. Is there someone we are still holding a grudge against? Is there hurt or resentment we have been carrying for too
long? Let us bring these feelings to God and allow Him to work in our hearts.

Sometimes, the hardest place to practise peace is not in the world around us, but in our own hearts and in our closest relationships. We may pray for peace yet continue to hold on to hurt. We may know that God has forgiven us yet find it difficult to forgive someone who has wounded us. Without realising it, we can allow our pride, anger, or disappointment to affect the way we treat those around us.

Maybe we need to pause and ask ourselves: Am I allowing the peace of Christ to shape my heart and my relationships?

Take a step towards peace. We cannot always change another person's heart, and reconciliation may not happen as quickly as we hope. But we can begin by bringing our own hurts and struggles before the Lord. Because Christ has first made peace for us, we no longer need to let resentment have the final say. With His help, we can choose to respond with grace, take the first step towards reconciliation.

Maybe we need to apologise, forgive someone, or reach out to a person we have been avoiding. It may not be easy, but even a small step can begin to mend a relationship and trust Him with what we cannot change.

This Advent, let us not only prepare to celebrate the birth of Jesus, but also allow His peace to fill our hearts, shape our responses, and be reflected in the way we live and relate to others.
devotionals.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus to bring us back to You and bring us peace. May the peace of Christ fill our hearts and be reflected in the way we speak, love, and treat others this Advent season. In the name of Jesus, Amen.
